title: Agastya's weapons
hook: before a great sage hands Rama new weapons, Sita asks whether he should be carrying weapons at all
carry: fire is kindled by being near fuel

segments.voice: Yesterday: your line, I'll protect you. The sages showed Rama the bones, and he promised to stand between them and the rakshasas.

They're walking between hermitages, Rama ahead with his bow, Sita in the middle, Lakshmana behind. The path is narrow, the trees close, and nobody has spoken for a while. Then Sita, quietly, starts to talk. She's been thinking about that promise. She doesn't doubt Rama's goodness. She's worried about something else. You vowed to kill the rakshasas, and they haven't done anything to you. I'm afraid of what weapons do to the person who carries them.
screen: `SITA STARTS TO TALK.` → `THEY'VE DONE NOTHING TO YOU.` → `WHAT WEAPONS DO TO THEIR BEARER.`

segments.voice: She lays out her worry carefully. Three faults come from desire, she says: speaking falsely, wanting someone else's wife, and violence without enmity, harming those who haven't harmed you. You've never done the first two. The third worries me. Then she tells a story. Once there was an ascetic so devoted that Indra, king of the gods, grew uneasy. So Indra came disguised as a warrior and left a sword with him for safekeeping. The ascetic took the trust seriously and carried the sword everywhere: to gather fruit, to bathe, to pray. Slowly, without noticing, he grew rough, then cruel, and lost his practice. Fire, she says, is kindled by being near fuel. Here in the forest, let's live the forest's way; at home in Ayodhya you can take up a warrior's duty again. I only say this out of love. Rama's answer is just as tender. You say this because you care for me. But a warrior carries a bow so no one in distress cries out unheard. The sages came to me for refuge, and I gave my word. I could give up my life, even you, even Lakshmana, sooner than a promise made to them. Two good people, two real concerns, and the text lets both speak. Then ten years pass, the text says, in the hermitages of Dandaka, and the road leads to the sage Rama has been told to seek: Agastya.
screen: `THREE FAULTS FROM DESIRE.` · `THE ASCETIC AND THE SWORD.` · `I SAY THIS OUT OF LOVE.` · `NO ONE CRIES OUT UNHEARD.` · then, large: `TWO GOOD PEOPLE, BOTH HEARD.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest empty in your lap and name one thing you usually carry: your phone, a worry, a grudge, a role. Imagine setting it down beside you for these two minutes, not forever, and breathe empty-handed; if it pulls at you, let it wait.
Agastya's weapons. Before the sage gives Rama weapons, Sita asks whether carrying them will change him, and Rama answers with his promise.
Your line: fire is kindled by being near fuel. Sita said it out of love, and Rama heard it that way. Day five hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Reciters give Sita's question about weapons in the Aranya Kanda its full length, and Hindu teachers who discuss it note that the text lets both her concern and Rama's answer stand.

fork.setup: you're Rama. Sita, out of love, asks you to set aside your vow to fight the rakshasas while in the forest. what do you say?
options: you're right, I'll give up the vow.
I gave my word to the sages; I can't take it back.
fork.reveal: Rama honors her concern, but says a promise to those who sought refuge is one he can't break.

original.note: Sanskrit agastya: the great sage of the south, whom Rama meets next.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama gets new weapons and that's that.
what it means: Sita first asks whether carrying weapons will change him.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 9–10 is a full dialogue: Sita's three faults and the sword parable, then Rama's answer about protecting those who seek refuge.

chat.says: Why did Sita worry about Rama's vow to fight the rakshasas?
options: She feared carrying weapons could change him, like the ascetic with the sword.
She thought Rama was too weak to beat them and would surely be killed.
She believed rakshasas could never be harmed by any human weapon.
chat.meaning: Sita feared violence without enmity, like the ascetic who carried Indra's sword and grew cruel. She spoke out of love, and Rama answered with his promise.

Agastya.meaning: a great sage of the south, whom Rama goes to meet

Indra.meaning: king of the gods, god of storms and rain

Dandaka.meaning: the great wild forest of the south in the Ramayana

rakshasas.meaning: demons of the epics who prey on the forest sages

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 9 (Sita's three faults; the ascetic and the sword)
